# String Algorithms

The structures from Parts II and III worked with arbitrary keys — anything you could hash, compare, or hand to a comparator. Strings are different. The order of the characters and the content of nearby positions both carry information the previous parts' structures threw away, and the questions you naturally ask about strings — where does this pattern occur, where does any of these patterns occur, how do I index a text so future queries are cheap, how close are two strings when they don't match exactly — don't admit the same answers as questions about unordered keys.

The arc of this part is a single parameter family. Each chapter trades preprocessing for query speed differently.

* **Brute force** (chapter 23) does no preprocessing and pays $O(nm)$ on adversarial inputs. It's still what `str.find` ships, because its tight inner loop wins on cache-friendly hardware whenever the average case matters more than the worst case.
* **Finite automaton matching** (chapter 24) compiles the pattern into a DFA — one state per length of matched prefix — and scans the text in $\Theta(n)$. Preprocessing is $\Theta(m \cdot |\Sigma|)$, and the construction is the conceptual bridge to everything that follows.
* **Knuth-Morris-Pratt** (chapter 25) compresses that DFA into one integer per state — the failure function. Storage drops to $\Theta(m)$, the scan stays $\Theta(n)$, and the chapter rebuilds chapter 24's DFA cell-by-cell from the failure function to prove the compression is lossless.
* **Boyer-Moore** (chapter 26) flips the scanning order. Reading windows right-to-left exposes a class of skips left-to-right algorithms structurally can't see — when the rightmost character of a window isn't in the pattern, you can shift past the whole window. Sublinear in practice on natural text.
* **Rabin-Karp** (chapter 27) stops comparing strings and starts comparing fingerprints. A polynomial rolling hash updates in $O(1)$ per shift; equal hashes trigger a verification step. Las Vegas — always correct, sometimes slow — and the randomization-as-balance argument echoes the treap chapter from Part III.
* **Aho-Corasick** (chapter 28) generalizes the failure-function idea to a *trie* of patterns, scanning the text once and reporting every match of every pattern. The algorithm `grep -F` actually ships.
* **Suffix arrays + LCP** (chapter 29) preprocess the *text* instead of the pattern. Every substring of a text is a prefix of some suffix, so the sorted suffix array reduces pattern search to a binary search. Manber-Myers builds in $O(n \log^2 n)$ and Kasai computes LCPs in $O(n)$.
* **Edit distance and alignment** (chapter 30) drops exact matching. The DP grid of prefix-pair distances costs $O(nm)$ to fill, and the same grid handles longest-common-subsequence and longest-common-substring with small changes to the per-cell recurrence. Part VI's chapter on dynamic programming reaches back to this one rather than re-implementing.

Three patterns recur across the eight chapters. Preprocessing-versus-query is the part's organizing axis — every chapter sits at a different point on the curve. Automata are the universal lens — the DFA from chapter 24 is the conceptual ancestor of every left-to-right matcher in the part and most of the right-to-left ones too. And randomization at the boundary — Rabin-Karp's rolling hash, like the treaps from Part III — buys a different cost shape by making the worst case statistically unreachable. Part V picks up where Aho-Corasick leaves off: the trie was already a graph, and the next eight chapters let the edges go anywhere.
